name: Erik Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent Brookfold Farm, about 160 hectares, from a pension fund that's never once set foot on it. Most days start at six with the sheep, around 600 ewes, then whatever the barley needs, then fixing whatever broke yesterday. My tractor's a 1998 Ford I keep alive with parts from a scrapyard in Kellby. I like lambing, honestly, even the nights. What I don't like is the paperwork and the rent review letters.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The landlord's agent, a young lad called Pryce with a tablet. He walks the fields twice a year and talks about yield per hectare like the ewes are a spreadsheet. My partner Lena works as a teaching assistant, so we get by, but the tenancy is up for renewal in 2028 and that sits in my stomach. Noah's twelve and Ivy's nine, and they both think the farm is ours. It isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that's the one I'd pick if anyone asked me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the mart: told you so. All this talk about robots in the fields and it turned out to be another gadget for the people who already had money. I'd probably put a smug comment under the farmers' union post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I keep my head down and keep paying rent that goes up every three years anyway. AI was never the real problem for me. The problem is that the land belongs to people who don't farm it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'm doing. Lamb in March, shear in June, sell the barley through the co-op store in Kellby. Maybe I'd finally replace the gearbox on the Ford, about 2,000 if I can find a used one. I'd keep going to union meetings because the rent fight doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. A bit of me would also feel daft for how much I worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use any of the AI tools that did turn up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Lena uses one to write school reports and she says it's handy, fine, good for her. I don't want a machine telling me when a ewe's going to lamb when I can see it in the ewe's eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the real problem is ownership. Would the union fight look different in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, and that's sort of the point. It'd be the same fight we've had since my grandad's time. Tenants against landlords, small against big.

S0.say: I told you so. All this talk about robots in the fields, and it turned out to be another gadget for the people who already had money.
S0.think: AI was never my real problem. The problem is that the land I work belongs to a pension fund that puts the rent up every three years.
S0.do: Carries on with the same calendar of lambing, shearing and selling barley through the co-op. Replaces the tractor gearbox for about 2,000 if he can find one used, and keeps going to union meetings.
S0.feel: Relief, with a little embarrassment about how much he worried.
S0.quote: I don't want a machine telling me when a ewe's going to lamb when I can see it in the ewe's eyes.
S0.fieldNote: Erik turned the conversation to land ownership almost straight away. For him, technology is a side issue next to who owns the farm. He refuses AI tools even when they're harmless, and seems proud of that.

steps.text: Lamb in March, shear in June and sell the barley through the Kellby co-op
Replace the 1998 Ford tractor's gearbox if a used one turns up for about 2,000
Keep going to farmers' union meetings, because the tenants' rent fight goes on

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That one's closer to what I actually see coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say it needs rules. If the big estates get robot sprayers and drone shepherds, the tenants get squeezed out, and someone in government has to stop that. I'd say that at the union branch and I'd sign whatever petition goes round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Pryce would love it. A robot-run farm doesn't ask for a new roof on the lambing shed. If the fund can merge Brookfold with the next two farms and run it with one manager and a fleet of machines, they'll do it at the 2028 renewal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting away an extra 150 a month, which hurts, and we'd skip the summer week at Lena's sister's caravan. I'd push the union branch to bring a tenant rights motion to the regional meeting by spring. And I'd write to our local representative, which I've never done, asking for long tenancies to be protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicking, but it's like hearing a noise in the engine you can't place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning the new machines yourself, to make yourself harder to replace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know I should say yes. But I'm 43 and I've never even used one of those chat things, and I don't want to start learning to babysit a robot that's there to replace me. Maybe if the union ran a course and paid for the time, I'd go. Maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noah and Ivy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing yet. Noah asked me last month if he'd get the farm one day and I said we'll see. I'd keep saying we'll see until I actually know.

S1.say: This needs rules. If the big estates get robot sprayers and drone shepherds, the tenants get squeezed out, and someone in government has to stop that.
S1.think: A robot-run farm doesn't ask for a new roof on the lambing shed. If the fund can merge Brookfold with the next two farms and run it with machines, they'll do it at the 2028 renewal.
S1.do: Saves an extra 150 a month and cancels the family's summer week away. Pushes his union branch to table a tenant rights motion by spring and writes to his local representative for the first time.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing an engine noise he can't place.
S1.quote: I don't want to start learning to babysit a robot that's there to replace me.
S1.fieldNote: Erik admits he probably should learn the new machines, then refuses anyway. His fear is not the robots themselves but what the landowner can do with them. He's keeping the truth from his son with 'we'll see'.

steps.text: Put away an extra 150 a month, even though it hurts
Skip the family's summer week at his sister-in-law's caravan
Push the union branch to take a tenant rights motion to the regional meeting by spring
Write to the local representative for the first time, asking to protect long tenancies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. That's the renewal date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a scandal, and I'd mean it. The government let a handful of companies decide the future of everyone who works with their hands, and nobody asked us. I'd be shouting it at the union hall and probably outside the regional office with a placard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? It means I lose the farm. The tenancy ends in 2028, the robots are ready in 2028, and Pryce won't even need to make an argument. I don't have the money to buy machines, and I don't have the will to be the man who runs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first month I'd sit down with Lena and go through every bill. The car loan goes, we sell the second car, the kids' swimming stops. I'd get the union to demand a moratorium, meaning a legal pause, on ending tenancies for automation. And I'd ask the farm support office what help exists, though I doubt anything would be ready in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the day my dad sold his herd. Angry underneath that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the day look like when the letter from the fund arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd read it at the kitchen table before Lena gets home. Then I'd go out and do the evening feed because the sheep still need feeding. On the day the landlord's notice came, I think I'd count the sheep twice, like that changes anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the farm goes, where would you look for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are a few other farms around Kellby, but they'd be going robot too, that's the whole picture you just gave me. Maybe the council would need people for something. I honestly don't know, and I don't like not knowing.

S2.say: It's a scandal. The government let a handful of companies decide the future of everyone who works with their hands, and nobody asked us.
S2.think: It means I lose the farm. The tenancy ends in 2028, the robots are ready in 2028, and I don't have the money to buy machines or the will to run them.
S2.do: Goes through every bill with Lena in the first month, sells the second car and stops the kids' swimming. Pushes the union to demand a legal pause on ending tenancies for automation, and asks the farm support office for help.
S2.feel: Sick and angry, like the day his father sold his herd.
S2.quote: On the day the landlord's notice came, I think I'd count the sheep twice, like that changes anything.
S2.fieldNote: The 2028 tenancy renewal turns this scenario personal for Erik. He's clear about who he blames: government and the big tech companies. The image of counting the sheep twice was quiet but striking; he has no plan for after the farm.

steps.text: Go through every bill with Lena, sell the second car and stop the kids' swimming
Get the union to demand a legal pause on ending farm tenancies for robots
Protest outside the regional office with a placard against how AGI was let in
Ask the farm support office what help exists for tenants about to lose a farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That gets me past one renewal, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, we need laws, but I'd also say we've got a few years to get them. I'd be telling the younger tenants at the branch to organise now, not when the robots are in the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years buys me one more tenancy at most, if the fund doesn't break it early. It doesn't change who I am. I won't turn into a robot technician at 46, and I know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign the 2028 renewal for whatever term they offer and try to get it in writing that they can't end it early for automation. I'd build the savings up to six months, so about 300 a month extra, by selling the oldest ewes earlier. And I'd go to every union meeting, because with five years there's actually time for a campaign to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's room to breathe. It feels like a fight I could at least join.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years you said you'd lose the farm. What does the extra three years actually change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes the kids more than me. Noah would be seventeen by 2031, old enough to choose something that isn't farming, and I'd want him to. With two years I'd be dragging them through it. With five I could at least get them pointed somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy any machine yourself, to stay in the game?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd rather put the money into the union fund. If the union wins the right rules, I won't need a robot of my own. If we lose, a robot wouldn't save me anyway.

S3.say: We need laws, but we've got a few years to get them. Younger tenants should organise now, not when the robots are already in the yard.
S3.think: Five years buys me one more tenancy at most. It doesn't change who I am, and I won't turn into a robot technician at 46.
S3.do: Signs the 2028 renewal and tries to get a clause against early ending for automation. Builds savings to six months by selling older ewes early, about 300 a month extra, and goes to every union meeting.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with room to breathe and a fight he can join.
S3.quote: If the union wins the right rules, I won't need a robot of my own. If we lose, a robot wouldn't save me anyway.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time didn't make Erik adapt; it made him organise. The real change he sees is for his children, who would be older and able to choose another path. He refuses to buy machines on principle and puts his faith in collective rules.

steps.text: Sell the oldest ewes early to save about 300 a month towards six months' cushion
Go to every union branch meeting and put spare money into the union fund
Back the union's campaign for laws stopping landlords ending tenancies for automation
Steer Noah, who'd be seventeen by 2031, towards a future outside farming

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 53.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where we have no excuse. Ten years is long enough to write proper laws for tenants and workers, and if we don't, that's on us and on the government. I'd say that at the branch and to anyone at the mart who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm still not going to change much. I'd farm Brookfold as long as they let me and hope the rules come in. Ten years is time for other people to prepare. For me it's mostly time to worry slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put Noah's and Ivy's education first, so a small savings account for each, 50 a month, for training or college. I'd stand for the union branch committee, which I've dodged for years. And I'd keep the ewes and the barley going exactly as I do now, and keep the six months' savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit ashamed, if I'm honest. Ten years is a gift and I know I'd mostly spend it standing still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Someone near retirement might feel safe with ten years. Do you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, because 53 isn't retirement. I'd have ten years of not working before any pension, and no farm. That's the bit nobody talks about with people my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You called it a gift and said you'd stand still. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. I'm not proud of it. I'll fight for everyone else's future in a meeting room and then go home and do exactly what I did yesterday.

S4.say: This is the one where we have no excuse. Ten years is long enough to write proper laws for tenants and workers, and if we don't, that's on us and on the government.
S4.think: I'm still not going to change much. I'd farm Brookfold as long as they let me and hope the rules come in, so for me it's mostly time to worry slower.
S4.do: Opens savings accounts for both children at 50 a month each for training or college. Stands for the union branch committee, keeps the six months' savings and farms exactly as now.
S4.feel: Uneasy and a little ashamed of standing still with so much warning.
S4.quote: Ten years is time for other people to prepare. For me it's mostly time to worry slower.
S4.fieldNote: Erik openly admits the gap between his public fight for others and his own lack of change. He points out that 53 is too young to retire and too old to start over. The ten years mainly shifts his focus to the children's education.

steps.text: Open savings accounts for Noah and Ivy at 50 a month each for college
Stand for the union branch committee he's dodged for years
Keep six months' living costs in the bank and don't touch them
Keep the 600 ewes and the barley at Brookfold going exactly as now

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no contest. It lands the same year my tenancy does, and I'd have nothing. What would help is a law that says you can't end a farm tenancy just to put robots on it, and some kind of income for people like me while we work out what's next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. Everyone asks if the robots can do the work. Nobody asks who gets the money when they do.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks if the robots can do the work. Nobody asks who gets the money when they do.
portrait: Erik Quinn, 43, rents Brookfold Farm from a pension fund and runs about 600 ewes and some barley with a 1998 tractor he keeps alive himself. He never uses AI and refuses to start, seeing the real problem as land ownership rather than technology. He is calm if AI stalls, uneasy at steady change and alarmed by fast AGI that lands the same year his tenancy ends. Extra warning time doesn't make him retrain; it pushes him further into union work and into planning for his children's futures.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it arrives the same year his farm tenancy is up for renewal.
whatWouldHelp: A law stopping landlords ending farm tenancies just to automate, and an income for people like him while they work out what's next.
